Shared-decision making about a trial of nonsurgical treatment in the absence of red flags (locking, instability) should occur with patients with meniscal injuries, especially in the setting of degenerative tears.A

Although anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears are often treated with repair, especially in younger, active patients, there are no good data to show that surgery is superior to therapy and bracing, particularly in older and less active patients.B
Despite its potential benefits, meniscectomy may cause cartilage loss and increase the risk of osteoarthritis.B

Ligaments are defined as soft-tissue structures that originate and insert on bone. Ligamentous knee injury refers to the disruption of any one or a combination of the four major knee ligaments: anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), posterior cruciate ligament (PCL), medial collateral ligament (MCL), and lateral collateral ligament (LCL).
Menisci are soft cartilaginous structures that help prevent wear and tear on the knee joint.
Knee pain accounts for almost 4 million visits to primary care physicians annually.
Of these visits, about one-third are attributed to degenerative joint disease, 11% from meniscal injuries, 7% from MCL and LCL injuries, and 4% from ACL or PCL injuries.

Traumatic meniscal tears are seen most often in the second through fourth decades of life, often in individuals participating in sports. Traumatic meniscal tears often occur with ligamentous knee injuries.
The most common meniscal injury involves the posterior horn of the medial meniscus.
ACL injuries typically are non-contact injuries and occur as a result of a valgus force directed to a fixed knee (ie, unstable landing on the knee).

Some associated anatomical risk factors are associated with ACL injury, including a smaller ACL size, increased tibial slope, a smaller tibial eminence, presence of intercondylar notch stenosis, and varied sagittal condylar shape.
Meniscal injuries are usually associated with trauma in a twisting fashion but may also be degenerative.
PCL injuries are primarily traumatic, resulting from an anteriorly directed force to the flexed knee (ie, dashboard injury, fall).
Collateral ligament injuries occur from a varus or valgus force in a partially flexed knee.
Meniscal tears may be the result of degenerative changes in the meniscus or a sudden traumatic tearing of the tissue.
Cruciate ligament tears are due to excess forces on the knee joint in a fixed position.

In young athletes, a stretching and strengthening preexercise program is effective in preventing acute knee injuries. This program consists of warm-up jogging, cutting and jumping exercises, balance training with wobble boards, and strengthening of the quadriceps and hamstrings. Only 2% of athletes who use this program experienced knee injuries compared with 4.3% of control athletes (NNT = 43; 95% CI, 31-122).B Specific exercises may reduce ACL injury in teenage girls.
Studies of prophylactic knee bracing do not consistently demonstrate a reduction in knee injuries in football players.B
McMurray maneuver and joint line testing can be helpful in detecting meniscal injuries.C
Internal derangment should be considered in patients with a history of knee trauma and effusion. Rate of effusion should be considered.C
The Lachman test is the most effective clinical test of the ACL.C
MRI is effective for diagnosing meniscal and cruciate ligament pathology.C

The typical mechanism for meniscal injury involves twisting the knee while stationary. After meniscal injuries, swelling occurs after a few hours, and the patient complains of pain while ascending/descending stairs. Typical examination findings in patients with meniscal injuries include joint line tenderness and an abnormal McMurray test.

The “Thessaly test” has only been studied in a single setting, but had excellent accuracy for diagnosis of meniscal injuries. The test is done by having the patient stand barefoot on the normal leg, holding the examiner’s hands for balance. The patient bends the knee of the standing leg 5 degrees and rotates the knee and body in and out three times. The test is repeated with the knee flexed 20 degrees and then performed on the injured leg. Patients with a tear have pain at the joint line on the side of the tear.
The likelihood of a complete ACL tear increases with the presence of each of the following: effusion, popping, giving way, and an abnormal anterior drawer test.

The typical mechanism for PCL injury involves hyperextension of the knee while the foot is fixed or a direct fall onto a flexed knee. Patients with PCL injuries often have an abnormal posterior drawer test.

The typical mechanism for ACL injury involves medial rotation of the knee with a fixed foot. The patient may describe feeling or hearing a “pop.” Patients with ACL injuries often have abnormal Lachman, pivot shift, and/or anterior drawer tests.

Clinical factors and use of a prediction model is modestly useful to predict meniscal tears in primary care settings, although use of MRI as a gold standard is flawed given the high prevalence of abnormal MRIs in the general population.
The "duck walk" test is of limited utility in detecting meniscal tears.

MRI is helpful in diagnosing structural injuries such as meniscal injuries, ACL tears, and PCL tears. Ultrasound is sensitive but not specific. It is important to know that meniscal tears are seen in 35% of patients over 50 years, are more common in men, and fully 61% were seen in patients without any pain. Recent studies have confirmed a high level of MRI abnormalities in patients with no knee pain. In particular, meniscal lesions are seen in 35% of men and 15% of women and damage is similar in patients with and without pain. A study of asymptomatic individuals found that meniscal tears, almost all medial, were present in 30% of knee MRI images, and meniscal deterioration was present in 18%.

When using the Ottawa knee rule, order X-rays in patients with acute injuries having any of the following: older than 55 years; tenderness at the fibular head; isolated patella tenderness; inability to flex 90 degrees; inability to take four steps. This rule is 100% sensitive and 52% specific.

According to the Pittsburgh knee rule, you should order X-rays in patients with pain resulting from fall or blunt trauma who are younger than 12 years or older than 50 years. For other ages, order an X-ray only if the patient is unable to walk 4 steps. This rule is 99% sensitive and 60% specific.

When performing a diagnostic arthrocentesis, bloody effusions should raise suspicion for acute ACL or PCL tears. Arthrocentesis can facilitate clinical examinations when excess joint fluid is removed. Other causes of bloody knee effusion include peripheral meniscal tear, fracture, and patellar dislocation.
See Diagnostic Testing for discussion of Ottawa and Pittsburgh knee rules.

Patients with meniscal injuries should be given a trial of nonsurgical treatment (ie, NSAIDs, physical therapy), because no randomized trials have compared surgical versus nonsurgical treatment.A
Partial meniscectomy seems preferable to complete removal of the meniscus in meniscal tears that do not respond to conservative management.C

Although ACL tears are often treated with repair, especially in younger, active patients, there are no good data to show that surgery is clearly superior to therapy and bracing, especially in less active and older patients.B
PCL injuries can be treated by conservative management or surgical repair. No studies have been done comparing the two.C

Arthroscopic repair is the favored approach for athletes involved in cutting and pivoting sports. Patients who wear braces after ACL repair have reinjury rates comparable to those of patients who do not wear a brace.
Increasingly though it is clear that many young athletes will do well without reconstructive surgery for a torn ACL.
Adults with non-acute, unstable ACL injuries may do slightly better with surgical repair but this difference may not be clinically significant.

The ACL SNAPP compared early surgery with rehabilitation in patients with non-acute ACL tear. While crossovers from rehab to surgery were common (41%) both per protocol and ITT analyses favored surgery. The difference in knee function and pain were statistically significant but of borderline clinical signicance (8 points on a 100 point scale).
Though evidence is inconclusive, research shows that reconstructive surgery for a torn ACL may be more cost effective than conservative treatment.

Preoperative aspiration of posttraumatic hemarthrosis did not affect rates of subsequent surgery following intial ACL repair. However, performing preoperative aspiration did delay the onset of arthrofibrosis.
Functional recovery is similar in adults with ACL tear comparing surgical versus conservative treatments.

While surgery was often routinely performed for meniscal injury in the past, it is increasingly clear that many patients do not require surgery and benefit equally from physical therapy when comparing pain, function, and quality of life.

Exercise-based physical therapy was noninferior to arthroscopic partial meniscectomy for patient-reported knee function in mild to moderate degenerative meniscal tears, suggesting that physical therapy is the preferred treatment.

Arthroscopic meniscal repair is indicated in athletes who do not improve with conservative management (physical therapy, ice, NSAIDs, rest, bracing). Partial meniscectomy seems preferable to complete removal of the meniscus in meniscal tears that do not respond to conservative management.
Patients with no or mild osteoarthritis and a parital nontraumatic menisceal tear do not benefit from surgery.

The ESCAPE trial compared early surgery with physical therapy in 321 patients with non-obstructive meniscal tears. They found that surgery was equivalent to physical therapy for function and pain. Note that some patients starting physical therapy will progress to surgery.
A systematic review identified 9 RCTs and 8 previous systematic reviews. The authors concluded that outcomes for arthroscopy and nonsurgical treatment are equivalent for menisceal tears.
Acupuncture reduces postoperative knee pain.
Acupuncture is not superior to sham acupuncture for chronic knee pain.
Patients with PCL tears can be managed effectively by physical therapy and conservative management.
Medial and lateral meniscal tears are often clinically improved with physical therapy but may necessitate surgery if there are symptoms of instability and pain.
Patients with isolated injuries to the LCL and MCL can be treated successfully with physical therapy, bracing, and a home exercise program.
More research is needed on specific exercise programs for patients with isolated ACL injuries.
Physical therapy is equivalent to surgery in many patients with menisceal tears.
In patients treated with arthroscopy, approximately 6% will develop a DVT or symptomatic PE. See chapters on those conditions for treatment.
Despite its potential benefits, meniscectomy may cause cartilage loss.B
Patients undergoing ACL reconstruction should not return to cutting and pivoting sports for at least 5 to 6 months.C
Patients undergoing meniscectomy can return to the field of play within 6 weeks.C

Untreated ACL injuries can lead to instability, pain, and cartilage degeneration; 77% of untreated patients developed ACL instability 8.5 years after surgery compared with 0% in the nonsurgical group. Additionally, 55% of the surgery patients had no evidence of OA on imaging compared with 100% of the nonsurgical group.
ACL rupture was more common in symptomatic patients with knee OA than in those that did not have a previous ACL tear.
Meniscal injuries may become asymptomatic or continue to worsen with pain or symptoms of locking and giving way.
Patients recovering from ACL reconstruction should not return to cutting and pivoting sports for at least 5 to 6 months; 9 to 12 months is more typical.
Patients undergoing meniscectomy can return to the field of play within 6 weeks.
Meniscectomy may lead to earlier development of degenerative joint disease.

tr.td: Knee flexed to 90° and examiner palpates around the entire joint line: medial and lateral
Examiner flexes knee 90° while patient supine and does internal and external rotary motion; test positive with click or pain in medial or lateral distribution
Examiner holds patient at 30° of knee flexion and with one hand supporting thigh, uses the lower hand to attempt anterior displacement of the tibia; test positive when no end point is felt
Examiner stabilizes patient at 90° knee flexion and then attempts to translate the tibia anteriorly with respect to the femur
Examiner stabilizes patient at 90° knee flexion and then attempts to translate the tibia posteriorly with respect to the femur
